title: How to Get the Most Out of Your First Conversation With a Mentor
excerpt: Your first conversation with a mentor doesn't need to be complicated. Here's the simple 30–40 minute structure I like the people I mentor to use, and why coming prepared, asking good questions and leaving with clear actions can make mentoring far more valuable.
content:
One of the things I talk about a lot with people I mentor is how to make mentoring useful.

It sounds obvious, but having a mentor doesn't automatically mean you'll get much from the relationship. You can have a great mentor and regular conversations and still leave every session thinking, *"That was a nice chat, but I'm not sure what I'm supposed to do with it."*

I don't think mentoring should work like that. When I mentor someone, I like them to take some ownership of the conversation. I'm not expecting a polished presentation or a list of twenty questions, but I do want them to have thought about what they want from it and, ideally, to bring something specific to talk about.

A first conversation can be surprisingly simple. If you've got 30 to 40 minutes, here's the structure I like to ask people to follow.

## Start with where you want to go

I'd normally spend the first five minutes or so on goals.

That doesn't mean having your whole career mapped out. Most people don't, and I certainly wouldn't expect someone early in their career to know where they'll be in ten years. I want to understand what they're trying to achieve right now. Maybe they want to become a team leader, or they're struggling with confidence. Maybe they've just been promoted and aren't sure how to approach the new responsibilities, or they're trying to work out what their next step should be.

Mentoring works much better when the conversation has that context. If I know where someone wants to get to, I can help them think about the route. Without it, a mentoring conversation easily turns into a collection of interesting but disconnected advice.

So I'm not asking for a five-year plan, just an answer to a simpler question: *"What would I like to be different as a result of this mentoring relationship?"* Even if the answer changes later, it's a useful place to start.

## Bring me something you're actually struggling with

This is probably the biggest thing I'd encourage. Don't spend the whole session telling me how well everything is going.

If you've got a difficult situation at work, bring it. If you're struggling with a colleague, or you've been given feedback you don't understand, or you've made a mistake and aren't sure what to do next, that's exactly what I'd rather discuss. A real problem to work through is worth far more than twenty minutes of generic career development.

The mentee has an important part to play here. I don't expect them to arrive with the perfect solution, but I do like them to have thought about the problem first:

- What happened?
- What have you already tried?
- What do you think you should do?
- What's stopping you from doing it?
- What are you worried might happen?

With those answers, we're not starting from scratch.

I'm not there to make their decisions for them. My job is to bring some experience and perspective, ask questions they might not have considered and sometimes challenge the way they're looking at the problem. If I have a clear opinion about what I'd do, I'll say so, but I'll explain why, because in the end it's their career and their decision. A good mentor helps you make better decisions yourself.

## Ask what you should be learning

Once we've worked through the immediate stuff, I'd usually spend a few minutes looking further ahead. This is where I'd encourage people to ask things like *"Is there anything you think I should be learning at this stage?"* or *"Is there anything you wish you'd known at this point in your career?"*

The answers can be surprisingly useful. It might be a book, a course or a skill to develop. It could even be something unrelated to the original problem that will help in the longer term. Part of the point of a mentor is access to someone else's experience: you don't have to make every mistake yourself if someone has already made it and is willing to tell you what they learned.

That doesn't mean following every recommendation blindly. If I recommend a book, I'd expect the person to decide whether it's useful to them. The aim is to expose yourself to different ideas and perspectives, and a recommendation shouldn't turn into another checklist of things you have to do.

## Don't finish without deciding what happens next

The last five minutes are probably the most important. I always encourage people to finish by summarising what they've taken from the conversation and, more importantly, what they're going to do with it.

Maybe there's a conversation they need to have, or something they've decided to read. Maybe they'll try a different approach with their team, or they've realised there's a skill they need to work on. Whatever it is, I'd rather they leave with one or two clear actions than ten vague ideas.

This part is easy to overlook. A great conversation can feel incredibly productive and leave you motivated and full of ideas, but if nothing changes afterwards, it was just a conversation.

Agreeing next steps also gives us something to come back to. If we talked last month about a difficult conversation they were planning to have, I'd want to know how it went, what they learned and whether they'd approach it differently next time. That follow-up is how mentoring turns into a relationship instead of a series of isolated chats.

## Come prepared, but don't overthink it

If you're about to have your first conversation with a mentor, I wouldn't spend hours preparing. I'd think about four things:

- Where am I trying to get to?
- What am I struggling with right now?
- What could I learn from this person's experience?
- What do I want to do differently afterwards?

For a 40-minute conversation, that roughly works out as five minutes on your goals, twenty on a real challenge, five on learning and the last five agreeing what happens next. The timings just give the conversation some shape. What matters is that you come ready to take part.

When I mentor someone, I don't want them sitting there waiting for me to tell them what to do. I want them to bring their own thoughts, problems and ideas, so I can understand how they're thinking and help them challenge, refine or build on it.

Your mentor has experience you don't have yet. You have something they don't: you're the one living the situation, and you know your circumstances, ambitions and challenges better than anyone else.

So don't go into a mentoring session expecting your mentor to give you all the answers. Go in expecting them to help you find better questions.
